questions.subtopic: Major muscle groups and the roles of muscles
questions.question_text:
A footballer bends their knee before kicking the ball.

Using this example, explain how muscles work as an antagonistic pair.

points: Muscles can only pull / contract, so they work in pairs
The agonist (prime mover) contracts to cause the movement while the antagonist relaxes
Bending the knee (flexion): the hamstrings are the agonist
The quadriceps are the antagonist, relaxing / lengthening
When the leg straightens to kick (extension), the roles reverse: the quadriceps contract and the hamstrings relax
scheme.guidance: Max 4. Two marks for knowledge, two for correct application to the knee. Do not credit muscles 'pushing'.

questions.subtopic: Lever systems: first, second and third class
questions.question_text:
A basketball player rises onto their toes (plantar flexion at the ankle) before jumping.

Identify the class of lever used at the ankle and explain the advantage this lever gives the player.

points: Second class lever
The load (body weight) is between the fulcrum (ball of the foot) and the effort (calf muscle / gastrocnemius pulling on the heel via the Achilles tendon)
The effort arm is longer than the load arm, so it has a high mechanical advantage
So a large load (the body's weight) can be moved with relatively little effort, helping the player push off powerfully
scheme.guidance: The first mark is for the class. Do not credit the third or fourth point if the lever is identified as third class.

questions.topic: Cardiovascular and Respiratory Systems & Effects of Exercise
questions.subtopic: Short- and long-term effects of exercise
questions.question_text: Describe four long-term effects of regular aerobic training on the cardiovascular and respiratory systems.

points: Heart becomes bigger and stronger (cardiac hypertrophy)
Increased stroke volume
Lower resting heart rate (bradycardia)
Increased cardiac output during maximal exercise
More capillaries (capillarisation) around muscles and alveoli
Increased number of red blood cells
Stronger respiratory muscles (intercostals and diaphragm), so increased vital capacity / tidal volume during exercise
Faster recovery / lower blood pressure
scheme.guidance: One mark per correct long-term effect, max 4. Short-term effects such as increased heart rate during exercise score nothing.

questions.topic: Cardiovascular and Respiratory Systems & Effects of Exercise
questions.question_text: Compare aerobic and anaerobic exercise. Use examples from a game of netball or another team game in your answer.

levels.descriptor: Detailed, accurate comparison of both types, using equations or by-products, intensity and duration, with well-applied examples from the game. Accurate terminology.
Some accurate comparison, with at least one relevant example. Some terminology.
Basic descriptions of aerobic or anaerobic exercise, with little comparison or application.

indicative: Aerobic: with oxygen; glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water
Anaerobic: without oxygen; glucose → energy + lactic acid
Aerobic is low to moderate intensity and can be sustained for a long time
Anaerobic is high intensity and short duration
Lactic acid causes muscle fatigue and an oxygen debt (EPOC) after anaerobic work
Example aerobic: jogging back into position or moving around the court during a match
Example anaerobic: a sprint to intercept a pass or a jump to catch the ball
Team games use both; players switch between them
scheme.guidance: Compare means both similarities/differences should be referred to throughout. Level 3 needs examples from a game.

questions.question_text: Describe how to carry out the multi-stage fitness test (bleep test), and state which component of fitness it measures.

points: It measures cardiovascular endurance (aerobic endurance)
Two lines/cones are set 20 m apart
The performer runs between the lines in time with the bleeps
The time between bleeps gets shorter as the levels increase
The test ends when the performer can no longer keep up with the bleeps (e.g. misses two in a row); the level and shuttle reached is recorded
scheme.guidance: Max 4. Do not credit 'muscular endurance' or 'speed' for the component.

questions.topic: Principles of Training, Optimising Training & Preventing Injury
questions.question_text:
A 400 m runner wants to improve their performance over the next season.

Explain how the runner could apply the principles of training, including FITT, to their training programme.

levels.descriptor: Several principles accurately explained and clearly applied to a 400 m runner, with practical examples. Accurate terminology.
Some principles explained, with some application to the runner.
Principles named or described with little or no application.

indicative: Specificity: training must match the demands of 400 m, e.g. anaerobic interval sprints
Progressive overload: gradually increase the training load, e.g. more repetitions or faster times
Reversibility: fitness is lost if training stops, e.g. through injury
Tedium: vary training to avoid boredom, e.g. hill sprints, track intervals, circuits
Frequency: e.g. train 4–5 times a week with rest days
Intensity: high intensity, e.g. 80–90% of maximum heart rate for interval work
Time: duration of each session, e.g. 45–60 minutes
Type: the method of training, e.g. interval or fartlek training
scheme.guidance: Level 3 needs application to the 400 m runner, not just definitions.

questions.question_text:
Top-level football is heavily commercialised, with large sponsorship deals and media coverage.

Evaluate the impact of commercialisation on football.

levels.descriptor: Detailed knowledge with a balanced evaluation of positive and negative impacts on different groups, and a supported conclusion.
Some positive and negative impacts with some explanation; evaluation limited.
Simple points about sponsorship or the media, with little evaluation.

indicative: Positive: more money for clubs, facilities, wages and grassroots football
Positive: more media coverage increases the sport's profile and may increase participation
Positive: players earn more and can train full-time
Negative: kick-off times changed to suit TV, inconvenient for fans
Negative: high ticket prices and subscription costs exclude some fans
Negative: pressure to win can lead to deviance; sponsors may withdraw after bad behaviour
Negative: wealth gap between top clubs and smaller clubs, and between men's and women's football (although commercialisation has grown women's football)
Judgement weighing the overall effect
scheme.guidance: Evaluate needs both sides and a conclusion for Level 3.

questions.topic: Ethics, Drugs and Violence in Sport
questions.question_text: Explain why a sprinter might take anabolic steroids, and two risks of taking them.

points: Steroids increase muscle mass / strength / power, helping the sprinter run faster
They allow the sprinter to train harder and recover more quickly
Health risks, e.g. liver damage, heart problems, high blood pressure, infertility
Mood swings / aggression ('roid rage')
Being caught leads to a ban, loss of reputation, medals and sponsorship
scheme.guidance: Max 4: up to 2 for why, up to 2 for risks. Two risks are needed for full marks.

questions.question_text:
A coach is teaching a beginner how to perform a tennis serve.

Evaluate the use of visual, verbal and manual guidance for this beginner.

levels.descriptor: Accurate knowledge of all three types, applied to the tennis serve, with advantages and disadvantages weighed and a supported judgement for a beginner.
Some knowledge of two or more types with some application and evaluation.
Simple descriptions of guidance types with little application.

indicative: Visual: a demonstration or video of the serve; good for beginners as they can copy a picture of the whole movement
Visual: demonstration must be accurate; may not show fine detail such as grip or timing
Verbal: the coach explains key points, e.g. 'toss the ball high'; useful with visual guidance
Verbal: too much information can overload a beginner; harder to understand complex movements
Manual: the coach physically moves the player's arm through the serve; helps the beginner get the feel of the movement and builds confidence
Manual: the player may rely on it; it doesn't feel the same as the real movement at full speed
Judgement: visual guidance supported by brief verbal points is usually best for a beginner
scheme.guidance: Level 3 needs all three types considered and a judgement.

questions.question_text: Explain the possible consequences of a sedentary lifestyle on a person's health and well-being.

points: Weight gain / obesity, because energy intake is greater than energy used
Increased risk of heart disease, high blood pressure or stroke
Increased risk of type 2 diabetes
Loss of muscle tone, poor posture and weaker bones (e.g. osteoporosis)
Emotional effects: low self-esteem, depression, stress
Social effects: fewer chances to meet people and make friends through activity
scheme.guidance: Max 4. Each point needs to be a consequence, not just a description of being inactive.
